newsitem.title: UK: Group details biggest risks to Lloyds for '97.
newsitem.headline: Group details biggest risks to Lloyds for '97.

text.p: The biggest risk facing Lloyd's of London next year would be an earthquake in California causing $50 billion in insured damage and a loss at Lloyd's of one billion stg, said the Association of Lloyd's Members in an annual study.
The ALM warned Names -- the traditional individual investors in Lloyd's -- that a trend that has seen the amount of insured losses increase over the past 10 years may be here to stay.

Citing figures prepared for the Chicago Board of Trade, it noted annual catastrophe losses in the United States have been rising since 1950, and suggested the main reason for this was the steady growth in the insurance value of property in hurricane prone areas like Florida on the U.S. East Coast.
"It follows that the frequency and severity of catastrophe losses may have increased permanently," said the ALM report.

Lloyd's completed in September a recovery plan to reinsure more than eight billion pounds of losses, caused in part by a series of natural disasters during 1988-1992, into a new company called Equitas.
It now requires that disaster scenarios are built into syndicate business plans, which means members' agents have been able to calculate the consequences for Names.

Drawing on data supplied by Syndicate Underwriting Research Limited, which has assumed capacity next year of 9.7 billion stg, the ALM said that a U.S. East Coast windstorm causing $50 billion in damage represented the second single biggest risk to Lloyd's
This would probably lead to a loss of 0.75 billion stg after reinsurance and without taking account of profits elsewhere.

A European storm or flood causing 10 billion stg of insured damage would mean a 0.6 billion stg loss. A collision between one of the world's biggest oil tankers and a cruise ship would cost Lloyd's similar amount.
An earthquake in Japan causing $8.0 billion damage could cost the market 0.5 billion stg, a North Sea oil disaster 0.3 billion and a "jumbo" jet collision over New York 0.2 billion.
